outcome.technical: _locks.py: new kernel_lock_refusal(exc) -> LOCK_HELD | LOCK_REFUSED (the one errno reading, over _HELD_ERRNOS now a frozenset); _try_lock returns (LOCK_TAKEN|LOCK_HELD|LOCK_REFUSED, exc). _dir_mutex waits out LOCK_HELD to MUTEX_SECONDS as before, and on LOCK_REFUSED runs the body without the mutex, yielding the _unmutexed() sentence (None when held). _claim and _take_over add a `mutex` key ONLY when that sentence exists, so the three-key answer the existing pins compare stays byte-equal; _remove_claim returns (verdict, unheld); acquire (fresh take, takeover, already-gone), _replace_own and release print `             mutex: <sentence>` via _say_unmutexed. The mutex file opens through _open_mutex: O_RDWR|O_CREAT 0o666, falling back to O_RDONLY|O_CREAT on PermissionError. Deviation from the brief's literal O_RDONLY: writing is asked first because Linux NFS emulates flock with byte-range locks and wants a writable descriptor for an exclusive one (flock(2) NOTES, from memory: not verified on an NFS mount here); a refusal there now degrades rather than erring anyway. The no-primitive error now says 'so no claim is changed here' instead of 'a claim is never changed without one'; the module docstring names the degraded mode. usage_ledger.py: imports _locks, removes _CONTENDED and the now-unused errno import; lock_month returns LOCK_UNAVAILABLE when _locks.kernel_lock_refusal(exc) == _locks.LOCK_REFUSED, so its answers for every errno are what they were (same held set). tests/test__locks.py: _MX_CHILD's plain racer wraps M._dir_mutex and writes <gate>.r2at on its first call; _mx_race starts the bound from it and returns `reached`; mx6 and mx7 require it.
